steps.title: Đọc
steps.heading: Intelligent machines and the future of work
steps.purpose: Đọc để tìm: hai phía của cuộc tranh luận là gì, và tác giả cho rằng điều gì sẽ quyết định kết quả?
text: Few transformations in modern economic history have been as widely anticipated, or as poorly understood, as the rise of intelligent machines. The World Economic Forum projects that roughly 170 million new roles will be created by 2030 while 92 million are displaced, a net gain that has encouraged optimists to speak of renewal rather than loss. Yet to describe a shift of this scale only in terms of totals is to obscure its human texture. What is unfolding is a seismic shift in how work is organised, and the tremors are felt first by those whose tasks are most easily codified.

The optimistic case deserves a fair hearing. Historically, technological upheaval has destroyed particular jobs while expanding overall prosperity, and there is little reason to think that this pattern has been abolished. Workers who are adept at learning, communicating and solving unfamiliar problems tend to move between roles with remarkable ease, and employers increasingly value such adaptability above narrow credentials. It is also true that many of the tasks now automated were never satisfying: few people mourn the loss of hours spent copying figures between spreadsheets.

The pessimistic case, however, rests on a different observation. Insecure forms of employment have become prevalent in sectors where algorithms allocate work, and for those who depend on them, income can be precarious from one week to the next. The disruption is therefore uneven in both timing and severity: a graphic designer may retrain within a year, whereas a fifty-five-year-old machine operator, with a mortgage and few savings, faces a far steeper climb. Skills that were valuable in 2015 can become obsolete within a single product cycle, and no individual, however diligent, can reasonably be expected to anticipate every change.

What, then, determines whether societies emerge stronger? Much will hinge on policy rather than technology. Countries that invest in education, portable benefits and income support can mitigate the worst effects and build resilience into their workforce, while those that leave adjustment to the market risk deepening resentment. An equitable transition is not merely a moral aspiration; it is a condition for political stability, because people who feel abandoned rarely support the innovations that disrupted them. The task, in short, is not to resist change but to ensure that the costs of change are shared as widely as its rewards, and that every worker willing to retrain is given a genuine route to do so.

steps.title: Tự viết
steps.prompt: Write one paragraph (100 to 130 words) answering: "What will determine whether automation benefits or harms workers?" Use at least one inversion, one cleft sentence, and three upgrade words.
steps.hint: Position, two factors, one inversion, one cleft, a formal conclusion.
steps.sample: The effects of automation will hinge less on the technology itself than on the policies that surround it.
steps.model: The effects of automation will hinge less on the technology itself than on the policies that surround it. It is the speed of retraining, not the speed of the machines, that determines whether the upheaval remains temporary. Rarely have workers been asked to adapt so often, and rarely have they been given so little support. Where governments invest in retraining and income protection, the workforce shows greater resilience; where they do not, precarious work becomes prevalent. An equitable transition is therefore not an act of charity but a condition for stability, because societies that displace workers without helping them rebuild erode their own trust.

steps.title: Nói phản biện
steps.prompt: Speak for 60 seconds. Someone says: "Workers who lose their jobs to machines should simply retrain; there is no need for government help." Respond: acknowledge the point, rebut it with reasons, and conclude. Use at least two upgrade words and one cleft or inversion.
steps.sample: There is some truth in that view, but it overlooks how costly and uncertain retraining can be.
steps.model: There is some truth in that view, but it overlooks how costly and uncertain retraining can be. Many older workers cannot afford to stop earning while they retrain, and rarely do employers offer the time. What this means is that the burden of change falls on those least able to bear it. It is for that reason that governments should help: an equitable transition mitigates hardship and builds the resilience of the whole workforce. So, rather than leaving workers to cope alone, we should share the cost.

steps.model: Let me be clear: I do not believe governments should slow automation, but they must manage its consequences. First, slowing technology would sacrifice real gains in productivity and safety. What it would not do is protect workers, because those who are adept at new tools would simply move abroad. Second, the real problem is the upheaval that follows. Rarely do displaced workers find new roles quickly, and precarious work is becoming prevalent. Some argue that a slower pace would give people time to adapt; to some extent that is true, but it is the quality of retraining, not the speed of the machines, that decides the outcome. So, the answer is to invest in an equitable transition that mitigates hardship and builds resilience.

steps.title: Bài luận có giờ
steps.prompt: Timed essay (40 minutes): "Governments should slow down the pace of automation to protect workers." To what extent do you agree? Write about 250 words (at least 230). Include a clear thesis, two developed reasons with evidence, a counter-argument with rebuttal, and a conclusion. Use at least four upgrade words and at least two C1 structures (inversion or cleft).
steps.hint: Plan for 5 minutes, write for 30, check for 5.
steps.sample: I only partly agree with this statement: governments should manage the consequences of automation rather than slow the technology itself.
steps.model:
I only partly agree that governments should slow down the pace of automation. While the disruption it causes is real, it is the support offered to workers, not the speed of the technology, that will decide whether the transition is fair.

The case for slowing automation rests on the uneven nature of displacement. According to McKinsey, the lowest-paid workers are up to fourteen times more likely than the best paid to need to change occupation, and few of them have the savings to retrain. Rarely do such workers find new roles quickly, and precarious work is already prevalent in sectors where algorithms allocate tasks. A slower pace, it is argued, would give them time to adapt.

Yet slowing the technology would carry costs of its own. Automation raises productivity, removes dangerous tasks and lowers prices, and countries that restrict it risk losing investment to competitors. What a slower pace would not do is address the underlying problem, which is that retraining is expensive, slow and poorly funded. Were governments to invest seriously in lifelong learning and income support, the workforce would show far greater resilience at any speed.

In conclusion, the pace of change matters less than who bears its cost. An equitable transition will hinge on funding retraining, protecting people between jobs and telling workers honestly which skills are becoming obsolete. Governments that do so can mitigate the upheaval without sacrificing the benefits of innovation.

steps.title: Nói 2 phút
steps.prompt: Speak for 2 minutes: persuade a mixed audience that a country should invest more in retraining its workforce. Open with a hook, give two reasons, use one piece of evidence, address one objection and end with a call to action. Use at least three upgrade words.
steps.hint: Hook, reason 1, reason 2, evidence, objection, call to action.
steps.sample: Let me begin with a simple question: what happens to a country when half of its workers' skills become obsolete?
steps.model: Let me begin with a simple question: what happens to a country when half of its workers' skills become obsolete? According to the World Economic Forum, nearly forty per cent of skills will change by 2030. That is a seismic shift, and it will not wait for us. First and foremost, retraining protects the people most exposed to displacement. Rarely do older workers have the savings to learn a new trade alone. Second, retraining protects the economy itself: a resilient workforce is the best defence against disruption. Some will say it is too expensive. Consider this: it is the cost of doing nothing, in unemployment and lost trust, that is far greater. An equitable transition will hinge on our willingness to invest now. So I call on this audience to support retraining, and to take a stand before the upheaval arrives.
